label: Last Glacial Maximum
note: Ice sheets at their largest; northern ice began retreating 20,000–19,000 years ago and sea level rose.

label: Holocene begins
note: Formal start of the current warm epoch, dated by counting annual layers in a Greenland ice core.

label: Farming begins, Fertile Crescent
note: People in the Near East began managing, then domesticating, plants and animals as the climate changed after the last ice age.

label: 8.2-kiloyear cold event
note: A short, sharp cooling that marks the start of the middle Holocene.

label: Mid-Holocene
note: Proxy records show a warm peak around 6,500 years ago; climate models show steady warming.

label: 4.2-kiloyear event
note: Abrupt drought across many mid- and low-latitude regions; chosen as the start of the latest Holocene stage.

label: Little Ice Age
note: Cold in many regions, but not everywhere at the same time: no globally synchronous cold period.

label: Watt's steam-engine patent
note: Watt patents the separate condenser, which made steam engines efficient enough to power factories: the Industrial Revolution gathers pace.

label: Tambora erupts
note: The largest eruption in recorded history; 1816 became the 'year without a summer' in Europe and North America.

label: Fourier: the atmosphere keeps Earth warm
note: Joseph Fourier argues that the atmosphere keeps Earth warmer than it would otherwise be: an idea later called the greenhouse effect.

label: Global temperature record begins
note: 1850–1900 is the reference used to measure warming since pre-industrial times.

label: Foote: CO₂ warms in sunlight
note: Eunice Foote finds a jar of CO₂ heats more in sunlight than one of common air, and suggests more CO₂ would warm the Earth.

label: Tyndall measures heat-trapping gases
note: Lab experiments show water vapour and CO₂ absorb heat radiation.

label: Krakatau erupts
note: Global temperatures were lower by up to 0.5 °C the following year; they returned to normal by 1888.

label: Arrhenius calculates CO₂ warming
note: The first calculation of how much more CO₂ would warm the Earth.

label: First powered flight
note: The Wright brothers fly 12 seconds at Kitty Hawk.

label: Callendar links warming to fuel
note: Argues that burning fossil fuels has already raised CO₂, and estimates that this explains much of the observed warming.

label: Great Acceleration
note: After 1950 energy use, population, economies and atmospheric CO₂ all rise steeply.

label: Revelle & Suess: CO₂ in the air may rise 20–40%
note: They find the oceans have taken up most fuel CO₂ so far, but expect CO₂ in the air to rise 20–40% in coming decades as fuel burning grows.

label: CO₂ measurements at Mauna Loa begin
note: The first day's reading of Charles Keeling's record is 313 ppm.

label: Teller warns oil industry about CO₂
note: At an oil-industry centenary symposium, physicist Edward Teller warns that fuel CO₂ could warm the climate.

label: US science advisers warn of CO₂
note: A report to President Johnson projects CO₂ about 25% above its 19th-century level by 2000 and warns of climate change.

label: First credible computer calculation of CO₂ warming
note: Manabe and Wetherald calculate about 2.3 °C of warming from doubled CO₂ (one-dimensional model).

label: Report for oil industry warns of warming
note: A Stanford Research Institute report for the American Petroleum Institute says “significant temperature changes are almost certain to occur by the year 2000”.

label: Moon landing
note: Apollo 11: the first people on the Moon.

label: Total's magazine explains CO₂ warming
note: An article in Total's company magazine, by an outside geographer, explains warming from rising CO₂.

label: Oil crisis
note: The Arab oil embargo; emissions dip (computed from our data).

label: Exxon's projections matched reality
note: A 2023 study finds 63–83% of Exxon scientists' warming projections were accurate (depending on the measure).

label: Exxon scientist briefs top management
note: Exxon scientist James Black tells the management committee there is general scientific agreement that CO₂ from fossil fuels is the most likely way humans are influencing the climate; doubling it could warm the globe by 1–3 °C by 2050.

label: Charney report
note: US scientists put warming from doubled CO₂ at about 3 °C, give or take 1.5 °C.

label: Oil industry CO₂ task force briefed
note: A consultant tells the American Petroleum Institute's CO₂ and Climate Task Force, with members from Exxon, Texaco and Sohio, to expect about 2.5 °C of global warming by 2038 if CO₂ keeps growing at 3% a year, an estimate he calls subject to large error.

label: Exxon's internal CO₂ primer
note: An internal Exxon review estimates that doubling CO₂ could raise global temperature by about 1.3–3.1 °C.

label: Montreal Protocol
note: Phased out ozone-destroying gases such as CFCs, which are also strong greenhouse gases.

label: IPCC set up
note: Set up by WMO and UNEP to assess climate science for governments.

label: Hansen tells US Senate warming is detected
note: “…the greenhouse effect has been detected, and it is changing our climate now.”

label: Shell's confidential greenhouse report
note: Written in 1986 and issued in 1988: notes that fuels sold by the Shell Group made up about 4% of global CO₂ emissions from burning fuels in 1984, and warns of large climate changes.

label: Berlin Wall falls
note: The end of the Cold War; the Soviet Union dissolves two years later.

label: Soviet Union collapses
note: Russia's fossil CO₂ fell 42% from 1990 to 1998; world emissions dipped only briefly (computed from our data).

label: Pinatubo erupts
note: About 20 million tonnes of sulphur dioxide reached the stratosphere; Earth's surface cooled for about three years, by about 0.5 °C on average (up to about 0.7 °C at the peak).

label: UN climate convention
note: Adopted in May 1992 and signed at the Rio Earth Summit; in force since 1994.

label: Kyoto Protocol
note: The first treaty with binding greenhouse-gas emission targets for industrialised countries.

label: Paris Agreement
note: Countries agree to hold warming well below 2 °C and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5 °C.

label: COVID-19 pandemic
note: Fossil CO₂ emissions fell about 5% in one year, the largest drop in tonnes on record (about 2 billion tonnes), then rebounded.

label: First year above 1.5 °C
note: The first calendar year more than 1.5 °C above 1850–1900; the Paris limit refers to long-term averages.
